definition: Palatable means pleasant or acceptable to taste.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word palatable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know palatable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Dad's first curries were merely palatable; by December the family had stopped keeping a backup pizza in the freezer.
Edible promises only that you can safely swallow it; palatable promises you won't mind doing so.
Delicious outruns palatable by a mile: palatable food is eaten without complaint, delicious food is eaten without leftovers.

Tasty is plain, warm praise — the cook hears it and smiles. Palatable sits a full step cooler: pleasant enough to eat without complaint, and that is all it promises. A tasty stew wins requests for seconds; a palatable one just quietly empties the bowl.

Appetizing does its work before the first bite — the look and smell that invite you to start. Palatable is the tongue's verdict afterward: pleasant enough to keep eating. A dish can be appetizing on the platter and barely palatable in the mouth, or gray to look at yet perfectly palatable.

The wilderness course saves one lesson for the last night: the instructors serve boiled cattail root, plain.
It is, everyone agrees, palatable — you can eat it, nobody gags, a hungry hiker finishes the bowl.
Then the instructors add butter and salt from their packs and serve it again, and the lesson lands: survival food and supper are two ingredients apart.
Palatable is the quietest praise food can earn: it clears the bar of pleasantness and stops climbing.
Below it sits edible — safe, and that is all; above it, delicious.
The word also moonlights outside the kitchen: a palatable plan or palatable truth is one people can swallow — the mouth's ruling, borrowed by the mind.
Palatable is the quietest of food praise — pleasant enough, no seconds requested — and it moonlights for ideas: a palatable plan is one people can swallow.
Its unit-mate potable answers a different question entirely: palatable asks 'is it pleasant?', potable asks 'is it safe to drink?'

When Camp Redwing hired a new cook, the director's instructions were modest: after last summer's revolt over burnt oatmeal, the food had only to be palatable.
By the second week the goal was met.
Campers ate what landed on their trays, and the kitchen stopped finding sandwiches buried in the trash.
Nobody wrote home about the meals, either.
The stews and casseroles drew no praise at the counter, and no camper ever asked what was for dinner tomorrow.
The director counted this a success.
Complaints had fallen to zero, and the nurse reported that everyone was actually eating.
The cook shrugged when a counselor thanked him.
Nothing fancy, he said -- just food nobody minds finishing.
